meta.description: Genuine Dostoevsky — but the line is Prince Myshkin's in The Idiot, and the famous English wording is Constance Garnett's 1913 translation.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The soul is healed by being with children'?
meta.ogDescription: It's real: The Idiot, Part I, chapter 6. Spoken by Prince Myshkin — and the English phrasing comes from Constance Garnett's 1913 translation.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This one is real. It is a line of dialogue in Dostoevsky’s novel The Idiot (serialized 1868–1869), spoken by Prince Myshkin in Part I, chapter 6 — and the exact English wording everyone shares is Constance Garnett’s 1913 translation. The Russian sentence is “Через детей душа лечится.”
answer.confidenceText: Located in the novel — with two honest caveats: the speaker is a character, and the famous English phrasing belongs to the translator.

source.heading: The passage

docMeta.dd: Part I, chapter 6 — spoken by Prince Myshkin
Serialized in Russian in The Russian Messenger, 1868–1869

source.excerpt: At first he used to shake his head and wonder how it was the children understood everything from me and scarcely anything from him; and then he began laughing at me when I told him that neither of us could teach them anything, but that they can teach us. And how could he be envious of me and say things against me, when he spent his life with children himself! The soul is healed by being with children.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ traced the line to The Idiot, chapter 6, and reproduces the passage from Constance Garnett’s 1913 Heinemann translation alongside the Russian text and the 1969 Henry and Olga Carlisle rendering.
We confirmed the original sentence independently: “Через детей душа лечится.” closes exactly that paragraph in Идиот, Часть I, Глава VI on Russian Wikisource ↗.

The same monologue — Myshkin, the village children, the jealous schoolmaster Jules Thibaut — sits at the same point in the Eva Martin translation on Project Gutenberg ↗, where the sentence is rendered instead as “Children soothe and heal the wounded heart.” The passage is Dostoevsky’s; the famous wording is Garnett’s.
source.excerptNote: Constance Garnett’s 1913 English, as reproduced by Quote Investigator ↗. “He” is Jules Thibaut, the village schoolmaster.

source.rightsNote: The Idiot was serialized in Russian in 1868–1869, and the English wording quoted here comes from Constance Garnett’s translation published by William Heinemann in 1913. Both the original text and this translation were published well before 1931, so both are in the public domain in the United States. (Later translations — the 1969 Henry and Olga Carlisle version, for instance — are separate works and remain in copyright.)

author.name: Fyodor Dostoevsky
author.heading: Who was Fyodor Dostoevsky?
author.bio: Fyodor Mikhailovich Dostoevsky was a Russian novelist, short-story writer and journalist whose fiction pushed into the political, social and spiritual turmoil of nineteenth-century Russia. His major novels — Crime and Punishment, The Idiot, Demons, The Adolescent and The Brothers Karamazov — are among the most influential in world literature, and his novella Notes from Underground is often called one of the first works of existentialist writing. Children recur throughout his work as a moral touchstone, which is part of why lines like this one travel so easily under his name.

misattribution.heading: What gets lost when it travels
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Dostoevsky is correct — which makes this an unusual case for a name that attracts fakes. But the line is almost always passed around stripped of the three things that actually explain it.

items.why: Dostoevsky wrote “Через детей душа лечится.” The memorable English sentence is Garnett’s 1913 choice. Henry and Olga Carlisle’s 1969 translation of the same line reads “Through children the soul is healed” — both versions are documented side by side ↗.
It is dialogue, not authorial commentary. Myshkin says it in Part I, chapter 6 while describing the Swiss village children he lived among — the sentence in its original chapter ↗.

items.who: Quote collections that print it bare
items.why: It circulates as a free-floating aphorism with no work named. The New Encyclopedia of Christian Quotations (2000) prints it under a bald “Fyodor Dostoevsky” with no source, and that is the kind of entry Quote Investigator was asked to chase down ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The verdict: real Dostoevsky, from The Idiot, Part I, chapter 6 — spoken by Prince Myshkin, in Constance Garnett’s 1913 English. Quote Investigator’s full trace ↗.

context.heading: What Myshkin was actually talking about
lead: Prince Myshkin has just come back to Russia after years being treated for illness in a Swiss village, and in Part I, chapter 6 he sits down with the Epanchin women and tells them how he spent that time. Not with doctors — with the local children. He passed four years among them as a kind of outsider, telling them everything and hiding nothing, until, as he puts it, they could hardly do anything without him and their parents turned against him.

The village schoolmaster, Jules Thibaut, was the angriest of all — jealous that the children understood Myshkin and not him. It is at the end of that complaint that the sentence lands. It is not a greeting-card aphorism about family life; it is a man who has been ill explaining what actually put him back together.
context.detailsSummary: Two English translations, two famous sentences
detailsBody: Constance Garnett’s 1913 translation gives the line as “The soul is healed by being with children” — the version that spread. Henry and Olga Carlisle’s 1969 Signet Classics translation renders the same Russian as “Through children the soul is healed,” which is closer to the word order of the original.

A third translation shows how much the phrasing is the translator’s work rather than Dostoevsky’s: the Eva Martin edition on Project Gutenberg renders the same sentence as “Children soothe and heal the wounded heart.” Same passage, same paragraph, same Russian — and a sentence nobody quotes.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator concludes Dostoevsky deserves credit for this statement, spoken by Prince Myshkin in The Idiot, chapter 6; the 1913 Constance Garnett translation reads "The soul is healed by being with children" and the 1969 Henry and Olga Carlisle translation reads "Through children the soul is healed"; the Russian is "Через детей душа лечится."

Quote Investigator's footnote cites the Garnett wording to: 1913, The Idiot: A Novel in Four Parts, trans. Constance Garnett, Chapter 6, Quote Page 65, William Heinemann, London; and notes The New Encyclopedia of Christian Quotations (2000, comp. Mark Water) printed the line under Dostoevsky's name at page 166.
The Russian sentence "Через детей душа лечится" appears at the end of Myshkin's remarks about the envious schoolmaster in Идиот, Часть I, Глава VI.

Project Gutenberg ebook #2638 is The Idiot translated by Eva Martin; in Part I, chapter VI it contains the Jules Thibaut passage and renders the sentence as "Children soothe and heal the wounded heart."

The Idiot is a novel by Fyodor Dostoevsky, first published serially in the journal The Russian Messenger in 1868–1869.
Constance Garnett was an English translator of nineteenth-century Russian literature and the first to translate almost all of Fyodor Dostoevsky's fiction into English.
Fyodor Dostoevsky (1821–1881) was a Russian novelist, short-story writer, essayist and journalist whose acclaimed novels include The Idiot.
